items.originalTitle: Who’s Afraid of Chinese Models?
items.summary:
Ben Thompson suggests the US should enact legislation explicitly allowing data collection for AI training as fair use and prohibiting terms of service that forbid model distillation, aiming to support US open AI models competing with Chinese counterparts. This proposal addresses the contradiction of AI labs banning distillation despite training on unlicensed data and advocates for a copyright policy that protects labs and promotes innovation.

Thompson also speculates that Alibaba's reversal to release Qwen 3.8 Max as open weights, after withholding Qwen 3.7 Max, may be influenced by a recent speech from Xi Jinping encouraging open source, collaboration, and sharing. Qwen 3.8 Max is a 2.4 trillion parameter model, nearly as large as the 2.8 trillion parameter Kimi K3, and has demonstrated creative outputs such as detailed illustrations with reasoning traces.

items.originalSummary:
Who’s Afraid of Chinese Models?

Interesting proposal from Ben Thompson that both addresses the hypocrisy of labs outlawing distillation against their models despite training on unlicensed data, and could help US open models compete more effectively with their Chinese counterparts:

The U.S. should pass a law that (1) makes explicit that collecting data for training models is fair use, and (2) bars terms of service that forbid distillation, for U.S. companies at a minimum. Stopping distillation — which is literally just querying the API — is nearly impossible; the U.S. should go the other way and lean into a new copyright policy that both indemnifies the labs and also guarantees that what they learned fuels further innovation for everyone else.

Ben also theorizes that Alibaba's decision to release Qwen 3.8 Max as open weights - a reversal from their decision not to release Qwen 3.7 Max in May - may have been influenced by a recent speech by Xi Jinping, who said:

We should seize this rare, historic opportunity to encourage open source, openness, collaboration and sharing.

And on the subject of Qwen 3.8 Max - a new 2.4T parameter model (nearly as large as the 2.8T Kimi K3) - here's a pelican it drew:

I particularly enjoyed seeing these notes in the (extensive) reasoning trace: "Could add helmet? No." and "Maybe add small bell? no." and "Need maybe add small fish in basket? Not necessary."

Via John Gruber

items.originalTitle: Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8, and Anthropic's (Potential) Unravelling
items.summary:
Moonshot Labs released Kimi K3 and Alibaba launched Qwen 3.8, two state-of-the-art foundation models reportedly close in performance to Anthropic's Fable 5, with plans to publicly release their model weights soon. These open models challenge top-tier developers by demonstrating that leading-edge performance can be achieved without proprietary restrictions, posing strategic risks to companies like Anthropic that rely on product differentiation.

The economics of foundation models involve high costs for training and inference, with companies choosing different infrastructure strategies ranging from leasing data centers to owning power generation. This affects margins and competitive positioning, as owning infrastructure can turn variable costs into fixed costs, enabling better scalability. Anthropic's focus on regulatory strategies and recursive self-improvement faces challenges due to its models' higher inference costs compared to competitors, raising questions about its ability to maintain market leadership amid increasing competition and potential price pressures.

items.title: Study measures AI-generated writing in 12,750 arXiv papers, finds about one-third flagged as machine-written by 2026 with field-specific variations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How we measured AI writing across arXiv, and where the measurement breaks
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed the full text of 12,750 arXiv papers from 2021 to 2026 using a calibrated AI writing detector, finding that the share of papers flagged as machine-written rose from a 0.4% false-positive baseline pre-ChatGPT to about 32% by mid-2026, peaking near 39% in early 2026. The study sampled ten academic fields and noted significant variation, with computer science showing the highest flagged rate around 65% and mathematics the lowest near 0.7%, though the latter's results are less certain due to detector limitations with mathematical notation.

The detector was calibrated to maintain a low false-positive rate using pre-ChatGPT papers as a control, and the analysis focused on full paper bodies rather than abstracts to better capture AI writing signals. Limitations include small control sample sizes per field, varying detector sensitivity to different AI models, and the inability to distinguish between lightly edited and fully AI-generated text. The reported figures represent a lower bound on AI writing prevalence, reflecting machine-like writing patterns rather than definitive authorship.

items.title: Cursor experiments with agent swarms to build complex software tasks, improving efficiency and coordination with a new version control system [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Agent swarms and the new model economics
items.summary:
Cursor conducted experiments scaling agent swarms to cooperate on complex tasks like building a web browser and SQLite from scratch, showing improved performance and efficiency over previous models. The system uses planner agents to decompose goals and worker agents to execute tasks, optimizing context management and coordination.

To handle the high volume of concurrent changes, Cursor developed a new version control system capable of processing around 1,000 commits per second, addressing unique failure modes such as split-brain design and planner contention through prompting and coordination mechanisms. This approach aims to generalize across diverse tasks and improve agent swarm scalability and reliability.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), a key standard enabling AI models to securely access external data and services, is receiving an update that changes how session IDs are managed. This update shifts from a stateful system requiring servers to track session IDs to a stateless approach, allowing servers to handle requests more flexibly and at larger scale without complex coordination.

The change addresses challenges faced by companies running MCP servers behind load balancers across multiple machines, where maintaining session state has been a significant technical hurdle. By adopting a stateless design similar to common web practices, the protocol aims to simplify infrastructure, reduce operational complexity, and lower costs for large-scale AI agent deployments. This update reflects ongoing efforts to improve the foundational infrastructure supporting AI interoperability beyond rapid advances in model training.

items.originalTitle: Flathub's AI slop ban looks like it was the right call
items.summary:
Flathub implemented a ban on AI-generated app submissions deemed low quality or poorly maintained, following analysis showing nearly three-quarters of such rejected projects were abandoned within months. This decision aims to preserve the platform's software quality and reduce reviewer workload caused by AI-generated code lacking human oversight.

Linux developer Evangelos Paterakis examined 120 AI-coded app repositories rejected by Flathub and found 88 were no longer actively developed, with many source codes deleted. The findings suggest that AI-generated apps often lack sustained developer involvement and innovation, reinforcing concerns about the value and longevity of such submissions.

The ban reflects broader debates about AI's role in software development, highlighting that generating runnable code is less challenging than creating useful, innovative applications. Flathub's move may encourage higher-quality contributions and more meaningful use of AI tools in open-source projects.

items.originalTitle: AI consciousness is a red herring in the safety debate
items.summary:
Professor Virginia Dignum argues that concerns about AI consciousness and self-preservation are misleading and encourage anthropomorphism, diverting attention from the real issues of human control and accountability in AI development. She emphasizes that AI systems, unlike autonomous extraterrestrial beings, are designed and constrained by humans, and consciousness is neither necessary nor relevant for regulating AI.

Dignum highlights that AI systems operate within the limits of computing machines and that claims of emergent consciousness lack explanation. She calls for conceptual clarity in AI risk discussions, focusing on how humans choose to design, deploy, and govern AI rather than speculative fears about machine consciousness. The article also includes letters expressing public concern about AI risks and the need for effective safeguards.

items.title: Federal judge approves Anthropic’s $1.5 billion copyright settlement over unauthorized book downloads in AI training [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic’s landmark $1.5B copyright settlement is approved
items.summary:
A federal judge has given final approval to Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement resolving a class action lawsuit alleging the AI lab illegally downloaded and stored millions of copyrighted books for training its models. The settlement will pay authors and publishers approximately $3,000 per work for an estimated 500,000 works involved.

The case stemmed from Anthropic acquiring books both legally and through pirate sites, with the court ruling that training AI on copyrighted text constitutes fair use but that the unauthorized downloads were illegal. While this settlement closes the lawsuit, it does not establish binding precedent, leaving ongoing copyright disputes over AI training data unresolved in other courts and cases involving companies like Google, Meta, and OpenAI.

items.originalTitle: Trump’s latest AI czar has already resigned
items.summary:
Chris Fall has resigned as director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), the agency confirmed, marking another departure following Collin Burns's brief tenure and David Sacks's earlier resignation. CAISI, which operates under the National Institute of Standards and Technology, is responsible for developing AI technical standards and assessing cybersecurity risks but has faced leadership instability since early 2026.

Fall was appointed three months ago after Burns left within a week amid tensions related to his previous work with Anthropic. CAISI has not been central to recent AI regulatory actions, such as the Commerce Department's temporary ban on Anthropic's models or the White House's new AI safety oversight program, which did not include CAISI. The resignation comes amid ongoing debates over AI regulation and competition, including concerns about Chinese AI models and calls for independent industry standards bodies.

items.originalTitle: Reverse-engineering is cheap now
items.summary:
I keep hearing anecdotes from people who used coding agents to reverse-engineer and automate devices in their homes.

I think this is an interesting illustration of the impact of the reduced cost of writing code.

Prior to agents, it was entirely possible to reverse-engineer home devices. The problem was the ROI - was it really worth all of that effort? More importantly, any experienced programmer knows that undocumented, unstable APIs like that may well change or break in the future. Is that initial work worth the effort if you're committing yourself to a frustrating cycle of maintenance in the future?

Coding agents change that equation entirely. The effort to get a simple automation working has dropped, as has the cost of trying and failing to get it to work. Since the code is so cheap, the idea of having to maintain it in the future - or throw it away and start again - carries way less psychological baggage.

items.originalTitle: What the New Kimi K3 Model Really Means for the U.S.-China AI Race
items.summary:
Thursday’s release of a surprisingly sophisticated new open-source AI model from Beijing-based startup Moonshot has ignited debate over whether China’s developers are erasing the gap with the dominant models from America’s AI firms.

There is little question that Moonshot’s Kimi K3 is impressive. The largest open-source model in the world, with 2.8 trillion parameters, it performed impressively on some AI benchmarks, topping a key coding leaderboard from Arena, for instance—ahead of both OpenAI‘s GPT-5.6 and Anthropic’s most powerful model, Claude Fable 5. 

Anastasios Angelopoulos, co-founder and CEO of Arena, said in an interview on The Information's TITV that Kimi K3 challenges the perception that Chinese open-source models are advancing simply by learning from top U.S. models, a process known as distillation. 

“This is the first time we're really seeing the narrative that breaks that mental model, that says that the Chinese labs might actually just be really good at developing models and not just distilling American intelligence,” Angelopoulos said.

items.summary:
It’s midsummer, but now is not the time to be on the beach. This week, we’ve got Alphabet, Google’s parent, and Tesla reporting second-quarter earnings, and the week after, we’ll get Meta Platforms, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple and PayPal, a company in the takeover spotlight right now. Of most interest, of course, is how Google, Amazon and Microsoft are doing on the AI front, both in their cloud businesses and in their other core operations of advertising, retailing and software, respectively.

On that front, investors have high hopes for Google. In the first quarter, a 63% surge in its cloud unit lifted Alphabet’s top-line growth to 22%, up 4 percentage points on the fourth quarter. Analysts think Google maintained that robust growth rate in the second quarter, with the consensus growth estimate at 21%, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. The cherry on top will be an expected huge gain Alphabet will report on its early stake in SpaceX, which went public in early June.
